transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Alternative polyadenylation, for Sunday, November 22.
Let's turn to Alternative polyadenylation, where long reads and isoform usage take center stage today.

First, a bioRxiv preprint from the Masamha lab. Using mantle cell lymphoma as a model, they combined short and long read RNA sequencing to catalogue alternatively polyadenylated and alternatively spliced transcripts.

Two disease genes, SOX11 and ATM, express short 3 prime UTR isoforms. But the short-read analysis found no widespread global 3 prime UTR shortening, a useful counterpoint to the usual cancer narrative.
Both canonical and non-canonical polyadenylation signals were used, and the authors verified specific ones experimentally. Long reads also revealed splice variants in genes like PTEN and EZH2.

Second, from the Gu lab in BMC Cancer: Nanopore long-read sequencing of paired liver cancer tumor and adjacent tissue, before and after incomplete radiofrequency ablation, analyzing expression, transcript usage and APA together.
Incomplete ablation reshaped the APA landscape. Oncogenes like SAE1 and SPINK1 showed 3 prime UTR changes that may stabilize transcripts and help them escape microRNAs.
The caveat is only five patients, and microRNA escape is a hypothesis that still needs functional testing.
Third, a bioRxiv atlas from the Wang lab mapping age-associated transcript usage in mouse brain, liver and adipose, in natural aging and in Ercc1 progeroid mice.
Only about 37 to 43 percent of isoform switches altered predicted coding sequence, so most look regulatory. And 3 prime UTRs lengthened with age in brain but shortened in adipose.
Quickly, three more. The Bouschet lab in iScience shows three-week mouse brain organoids reproduce most of the neural splicing and polyA site events seen in vivo.
A Tao lab preprint on bioRxiv reports a circular RNA that pulls the repressor PUM2 away from the Nt3 3 prime UTR, driving diabetic neuropathic pain in mice.

And a Roy lab preprint on Research Square predicts that colorectal cancer risk variants in 3 prime UTRs disrupt microRNA sites, checked in 453 Hispanic All of Us participants, though so far only computationally.
The takeaway: long reads are sharpening APA maps, and 3 prime UTR length changes look context specific rather than following one universal shortening rule.
